claims.statement: The Rust server is authoritative for authentication, permissions, game state, turns, time, randomness, and rewards.
Account identity and persona identity are separate, and social or game surfaces expose personas rather than account ownership.
REST/JSON is the durable command and query interface; WebSocket notifications are advisory and cursor synchronization is the recovery source of truth.
HTTP and WebSocket handlers translate transport data while domain modules own authorization and invariants.

Authentication and MFA, persona social state and inboxes, durable synchronization, exact-version compiled game sessions, canonical cartridges, trusted rendering, deterministic SDK/release verification, signed catalog policy, and secure local import are implemented; public session creation, challenges, results, playable rules, main-client cartridge launch, and remote providers remain later work.
Registration creates an account credential identity only and does not create or expose a persona.

Device-session JSON omits account ownership and token digests; password login either returns a new session or an MFA challenge, and authenticated account-level operations do not create a persona identity.
The current local bearer-token slice requires production TLS and distributed login throttling before public deployment.
Authenticated persona creation, inventory, and editing derive the private account owner from a validated session, and owner mutation uses both account and persona IDs.
Persona responses expose only seven public profile fields, while exact canonical handle lookup is intentionally public and does not reveal the owning account.
The private-alpha product is game-first, while public message boards remain outside the current identity and first-alpha scope.

Optional TOTP MFA belongs to private account authentication rather than public persona identity, and successful factor verification gates creation of a new device session without changing existing sessions.

Public registration currently returns a distinct username conflict response, so production deployment must accept enumeration risk or introduce a separately designed verifiable private registration channel.
Social graph state belongs to public personas, but every acting persona is owner-scoped to the private account derived from the Bearer session and same-account personas cannot form social edges.

Accepted persona connections are mutual and block rows and inventories remain owner-private and directional, but a denied interaction with a known persona may still permit an indirect inference about block direction.

Private inbox authorization is persona-participant scoped: account ownership and peer read positions are omitted, history survives relationship removal or blocking, and new sends require an accepted unblocked connection.
Public inbox cursors are local to one conversation, so message sequence gaps do not reveal unrelated private conversation volume.

An owned persona's synchronization feed uses a retained persona-local cursor for durable REST recovery and explicit reset, while its header-authenticated WebSocket carries no domain payload and only advises the client to return to REST.

Compiled game definitions receive only bounded initialization or current-state, actor-seat, and command inputs and have no database, network, clock, session, account, or ambient-randomness capability in the runtime interface.

Durable game sessions expose persona participants rather than account ownership, pin their exact rules version and snapshot, and remain readable from PostgreSQL even when that version is absent from the current process registry.

The current server exposes a compiled-game catalog, participant-private session reads, and revision-checked commands but no public session creation; challenge policy, server-side cartridge ingestion and launch, and provider execution remain separate later slices.

A game command is a durable REST mutation whose success or matching replay returns only session ID, committed revision, and state; WebSocket notifications remain advisory and carry no command payload.

The portable-game direction uses immutable publisher-signed data-only cartridges rendered by trusted OmarchyGS components; raw publisher QML, JavaScript, native code, arbitrary shaders, and direct game networking remain prohibited.

Remote provider authority is not authorized: the compiled OmarchyGS runtime remains gameplay authority until a later production protocol, migration, and Constitution §10 amendment establish exactly one durable owner for each gameplay revision.

If remote providers are later enabled, OmarchyGS remains the authenticated broker and platform authority, discloses only a short-lived audience/game/version/session/scope-bound pairwise persona grant, and never sends account identity, reusable device tokens, credentials, or database access.

Production local cartridge tooling verifies inert signed packages, compiles bounded plans, exports a public SDK, verifies signed releases and catalog policy, and imports through a Linux descriptor-relative store without HTTP, SQL, dynamic-loader, or platform-credential dependencies.

A valid publisher signature authenticates cartridge bytes but does not grant resource trust: the renderer enforces profile counts plus per-raster and decoded-scene ceilings before publication, and QML independently enforces fixed plan and component boundaries.

OmarchyGS owns every executable QML component, trusted display preference, fixed origin and non-ready state, and future action dispatcher; cartridges supply only authenticated declarative nodes, bindings, assets, and unconfirmed action requests.

The legacy Ticket 015 store and preview output remain same-user developer boundaries, while Ticket 017's Linux secure store is descriptor-relative and rejects roots or fixed children not owned by the effective user or writable by group or other.
